condensedNotes.heading: Crime and Mental Disorder — Epidemiology

bullets.text: Violence is 4–6x more common in the mentally ill than the general population, but mental illness is an attributable risk factor in <10% of all crimes; personality disorder, alcohol and drug misuse are all bigger risk factors for violence than mental illness, as are male gender, age 15–30, socioeconomic deprivation and past violence history.

MacArthur study (Monahan & Applebaum 2000): violence in first 20 weeks post-discharge was 9% for schizophrenia vs 19% depression, 15% bipolar, 17.2% other psychosis, 29% substance misuse, 25% personality disorder alone. In the community, 10% with schizophrenia committed violence over 12 months vs 2% without mental disorder (5x); comorbid substance misuse raised this to 30%. Men with schizophrenia are up to 5x more likely convicted of serious violence (Wallace 1998); annual homicide risk with schizophrenia is ~1:3000 (men) and 1:33,000 (women).

Fazel & Danesh (2002): 62 prison surveys, 12 countries, ~22,790 prisoners — psychosis 3.7% (men), major depression 10%, personality disorder 65%; 1% of sentenced prisoners have an organic mental disorder.

Shaw (2006): 34% of homicides are related to a mental disorder, 5% linked to schizophrenia, 10% of homicide offenders have active symptoms at the time of offence. Brugha et al. (2005): psychosis is ~10x commoner in prison than the general population.

Penrose's Law (Gunn 2000; Kelly 2007): psychiatric institution occupancy rose inversely with prison occupancy, murder rate and live-birth rate. Related theories: 'prison psychosis' (incarceration as causal agent, disputed) and institutionalisation bias (Seddon 2007, following Foucault — prison as a means of confining undesirable/mentally-ill members of society).

condensedNotes.heading: Homicide, Filicide & Infanticide

bullets.text: Homicide is rare (1.2/100,000 UK). Homicides by mentally disordered offenders (MDOs) fell from 120/year (1980) to 20/year (2004), levelling at ~50/year recently. 10% of homicide convicts have an abnormal mental state (2/3 of these psychotic); annual risk of a person with schizophrenia committing homicide is 1:10,000 vs 1:150 for a violence conviction. Victims of MDO homicide are more often acquaintances/family than strangers.

D'Orban (1979) filicide typology — battering mothers (impulsive/loss of temper), mentally ill mothers (depression in ~100% of some series; psychosis/PD/dissociation), neonaticide (killing within first 24h of life, not covered by the Infanticide Act, often unknown to services), retaliating women (displaced spousal aggression), unwanted children (neglect/aggression from unplanned pregnancy and hardship), mercy killing (genuine suffering, no secondary gain). McKee & Shea (1998): psychosis 40%, major depression 25% among mentally-ill-mother filicides; borderline (5) and dependent (4) PD were the commonest axis II diagnoses.

Infanticide Act 1938 (UK): mother causes death of her child <12 months by wilful act/omission while the balance of her mind was disturbed by not having fully recovered from birth or from lactation effects. Incidence estimated 30–45/year in Britain (Marks & Kumar 1993), likely an underestimate (Resnick 1970); covert video surveillance may help identify high-risk cases (Southall 1997).

Murder-suicide is defined as suicide of the perpetrator within one week of the homicide; incidence 0.2–0.3/100,000/year. Depression is more common in murder-suicide (20–60%) than in homicide alone, while substance misuse/criminal history are less frequent. Classic profiles: a recently-separated depressed middle-aged man with firearm access, or an older male caregiver of an ill/debilitated spouse with new-onset depression and firearm access.

Parricide is rare (2% of all homicides); the perpetrator is usually a son aged 12–50 motivated by revenge for sexual abuse or financial gain (Seagrave 2009), typically a spontaneous act during a domestic argument against a background of chronic intrafamilial conflict (Shon & Roberts 2010).

condensedNotes.heading: Non-fatal Violence, Shoplifting & Kleptomania

bullets.text: Non-fatal assault occurs in ~1 million cases/year in England & Wales (2033/100,000), classified as common assault (apprehension of unlawful force), aggravated assault (attempted/actual serious injury) or battery (actual unlawful contact). ~9% of non-fatal violence convicts have schizophrenia, most intoxicated with alcohol at the time.

Only 3.2% of shoplifting cases involve mentally ill patients; shoplifting is linked to affective disorder, alcoholism and drug addiction. 24–30% of middle-aged female shoplifters may be depressed (Gibbens 1971). Shoplifting peaks in adolescence and most offenders do not reoffend once caught.

Kleptomania (ICD-10 F63 impulse control disorder): petty, impulsive theft without planning or accomplices. ~1–2% of shoplifters have kleptomania; most are women. ~50% have a comorbid personality disorder, most commonly paranoid then histrionic PD.

condensedNotes.heading: Arson & Fire-Setting

bullets.text: 1 in 4 fire-setters intentionally started the fire (=arson). The causal link between mental disorder and arson is weak; not-guilty-by-reason-of-insanity is used only for rare delusionally-motivated cases.

Geller & Bertsch (1985): 26% of psychiatric patients had a fire-setting history, 16% had actually set fires. Associated disorders: personality disorder, psychosis (8% schizophrenia, 11% bipolar among firesetters with mental illness), learning disability, intoxication (Rix 1994). Firesetters are typically young, unmarried, poorly educated, unemployed/unskilled males; arson is 2.5x more common in males, though the female proportion is rising.

Faulk's two groups: Group I — instrumental fires (means to an end, e.g. revenge, fraud, plea for help); Group II — the fire itself is the phenomenon of interest (e.g. pyromania). DSM-IV pyromania criteria: deliberate/purposeful fire-setting on >1 occasion; affective arousal/tension beforehand; fascination with fire; pleasure/gratification/relief during or after; exclusion of other causes; not better accounted for by conduct disorder or antisocial PD.

Juvenile firesetters make up >50% of all arrests; under-10s are usually motivated by curiosity. Fire-setting is commoner in girls among those detained in secure hospitals, often carrying an expressive/communicative meaning (revenge, jealousy, displaced aggression) related to property and relationships.

Recidivism ranges 4–20%; mental disorder is a poor prognostic feature (11% reconviction in MDOs vs 4% in non-MDOs). Recidivism risk factors: childhood firesetting, younger age at first firesetting, total firesetting offences, no concurrent charges, verbalised arson threats, setting fires alone, unmarried status, low IQ. Treatment is largely behavioural (aversive therapy, positive reinforcement, stimulus satiation); no established role for psychodynamic therapy.

condensedNotes.heading: Stalking

bullets.text: Mullen interviewed 6300 women: 15% had been stalked in their lifetime. 80–90% of stalkers are men and 80–90% of victims are women; the most common victims are women in their reproductive years with a prior sexual relationship with the stalker.

Mullen (1999) typology: the rejected (pursue ex-intimates for reconciliation or vengeance), intimacy seekers (believe the victim loves/will reciprocate), incompetent suitors (inappropriately seek a date/brief encounter despite poor social skills), the resentful (pursue revenge for perceived injury), and the predatory (stalking as part of sexual offending). Primary diagnosis in stalkers is often a personality disorder — cluster B (borderline/narcissistic/histrionic) predominates in ex-intimate stalkers; delusional disorder (erotomanic > jealous > persecutory), schizophrenia, affective and organic psychosis are common in stranger/celebrity ('star') stalkers. Mental illness is not a notable factor in those who stalk/attempt to assassinate public figures (Fein & Vossekuil 1998).

Effects on victims: PTSD in 37–60%, plus depression, anxiety, insomnia, somatisation and substance misuse. Risk factors for assault in stalking (Palarea 1999, Mullen 2000): substance misuse, offending history, male gender, threats of violence/suicide, personality disorder (narcissistic/antisocial), unemployment/social isolation, access to the victim, desperation, and non-compliance with treatment.

RCPsych 2007 survey: 22% of psychiatrists reported having been stalked; ~1 in 3 reported behaviours meeting the legal definition of harassment (~51 new victims/year among members). Stalkers of mental health professionals are usually males with a prior stalking history and an established axis I/II disorder under the stalked clinician's care, often motivated by a desire for greater intimacy. Prosecutions proceed under the Protection from Harassment Act 1997 (England & Wales); restraining orders can sometimes increase the intensity of stalking.

condensedNotes.heading: Sexual Offending — Epidemiology, Typology & Child Sexual Abuse

bullets.text: Most sex offenders lack a major mental illness (Grubin & Gunn 1991); <10% have a mental illness. Sexual offences constitute only 1% of all offences (likely an underrepresentation); perpetrators are almost exclusively male, and most have more than one category of deviant sexual behaviour.

Child sexual abuse: 80% of offenders against children are a relative (13%) or otherwise known to them (68%); the offender is usually male (90%), 1/3 are adolescents, and up to half of victims are related (girls are twice as likely to be victims). STEP project 'high-deviancy' offenders were twice as likely to have prior sexual offences and to have been abused themselves as children. 50–70% of paedophiles have another paraphilia; paedophiles are ~2.5x more likely to have physical contact with a child than to be purely voyeuristic/exhibitionistic.
Incest requires penetration by definition; sexual relations with step-relatives are not classified as incest in England (though Scotland includes them). 30% of reported incest is against children.

Indecent exposure may relate to exhibitionism or be secondary to alcohol, drugs, or rarely dementia/hypomania; the offender rarely communicates with the victim. Most stop reoffending after conviction; 20–30% reoffend, and reoffence-with-conviction carries a poor prognosis (high recidivism). An inhibited, 'guilty' exhibitionist (flaccid) is less risky than an angry, aggressive one (erect while offending).

Internet sex-offending typology: seeking emotional satisfaction (distressed, seeking solace), intimacy deficit (socially isolated) and hypersexuality. Offenders often have no prior convictions and most do not reoffend unless there is a past history of other sexual offending.

condensedNotes.heading: Sexual Offending — Reoffending, Predictors & the Abel Study

bullets.text: Abel study (1977–85, n=561 non-incarcerated offenders): 30% married, 40% had ≥1 year college, 67% targeted only females/12% only males/21% both; 56% engaged in non-incestuous behaviour only, 12% incestuous only, 23% both; boys were molested 5x more often than girls; most had multiple paraphilias, and in >50% paraphilic tendencies began before age 18.

75–80% of sex offenders have no previous sexual conviction (most convictions are 'first-time'); of those with ≥1 prior conviction, ~40% have more than one. Over 6-year follow-up, <10% are reconvicted of any sexual offence (rapists 19%, CSA 13% — Hanson et al. 2009), though reconvicted offenders commit very serious crimes; reoffence rate rises with longer observation.

Lowest reconviction risk: index offence against a child within one's own family (incest, <10% untreated recidivism). Highest: index offence against a child outside the family — those who molest boys reoffend more (13–40%) than those who molest girls (10–29%). Rapists are more criminally versatile than child molesters and more likely to reoffend non-sexually than sexually.

Lievore (2004) predictors of sexual reoffending: sexual deviancy/multiple offence types, diverse offending history, offences against boys (higher risk than girls), phallometric response to paedophile or nonsexual-violence stimuli, elevated Hare PCL-R score (Rice 1990), reduced self-esteem/impaired victim empathy or increased anger at index offence, own history of childhood sexual abuse, violent sexual fantasies, longstanding social isolation, occupational access to victims, sadomasochistic/paedophilic pornography use, and non-completion of treatment (associated with dissocial traits).

condensedNotes.heading: Sexual Offending — Assessment & Pharmacotherapy

bullets.text: Because sex offenders often deny intent, self-report is unreliable; penile plethysmography measures penile tumescence in response to visual/auditory deviant cues (Barker & Howell 1992). Finkelhor's 4-stage CBT model: (1) motivation to abuse, (2) overcoming internal inhibitions, (3) overcoming external inhibitions, (4) overcoming victim resistance — treatment covers the offence cycle, cognitive distortions, victim harm, fantasy modification, social/anger skills and relapse prevention.

Cyproterone acetate blocks testosterone receptors to reduce sexual drive (and, at higher dose, treats prostatic carcinoma — Bradford 1985); side effects include deranged LFTs, osteoporosis and gynaecomastia, and it can worsen depression — avoid with a history of severe depression.

Medroxyprogesterone acetate (main US anti-libidinal) induces hepatic testosterone alpha-reductase, increasing testosterone clearance. SSRIs and other antidepressants have a reported role in paraphilia treatment (initial buspirone case report in transvestic fetishism, Fedoroff 1988).

condensedNotes.heading: Domestic Violence

bullets.text: 31% of women survivors never tell anyone about domestic violence (40% of raped and 9% of stalked women don't disclose). Of those who told someone, 47% disclosed to a friend/relative; police were next most likely to hear (20%), then medical staff (10%). Police become aware of only 17–23% of women's DV cases and <1/7 of sexual assault cases — overall only 12% of individual assaults are picked up via survey. 1 in 8 women thought police involvement would make things worse.

Surveys including sexual violence and broader abuse indicate domestic violence affects 1 in 4 women at some point in their lives; women under 40 are most at risk (44% of all violent attacks are domestic-violence related).

condensedNotes.heading: Schizophrenia, Psychosis & Substance Misuse — Violence Risk

bullets.text: Two-type model of schizophrenia-related violence (Steinart 1998): Type 1 — organised delusional systems driving the violence, no prominent childhood conduct-disorder history, diverse offending before diagnosis, may be overrepresented among homicide offenders. Type 2 — disorganised clinical picture, childhood/adult conduct-disorder history, early-onset substance misuse, usually attacks a carer/acquaintance; most schizophrenia-related violence is Type 2.

Threat/control-override (T/C-O) syndrome (Link & Steuve) describes feeling threatened and one's mind being dominated by outside forces. The MacArthur Violence Risk Assessment Study cast doubt on this: neither delusions in general nor T/C-O delusions specifically were associated with increased violence risk.

>50% of prison inmates misuse substances and >40% misuse alcohol (vs 2%/4% in the general population); acute intoxication is linked with disinhibition/disorganisation and is associated with ~50% of non-fatal assaults and 66% of murders. Comorbid substance misuse raises the violence risk ratio in schizophrenia from 3.6x to 25x the general population.

condensedNotes.heading: Personality Disorder & Psychopathy in Forensic Populations

bullets.text: Offenders with PD mostly offend against known victims (including healthcare professionals); women with PD are more likely than women without PD to offend against children.

Prevalence: Any PD — 78% remanded men, 64% sentenced men, 50% female prisoners, 65% forensic patients. Antisocial PD — 63%/49%/31%/67% respectively, with a 10-fold increase in violence risk vs the general population. (See table for the full breakdown across BPD, NPD and paranoid PD.)

Psychopathy occurs in 15–30% of the forensic population vs 4% of the general population; PCL-R cutoff >25 diagnoses psychopathy. Factor 1 (callous-unemotional: arrogant, grandiose, glib, deceitful, lacking empathy/remorse, shallow/labile affect) is more heritable/biologically driven; Factor 2 (antisocial: impulsive, sensation-seeking, lacking planning, irresponsible, parasitic lifestyle) is more behavioural.

condensedNotes.heading: Learning Disability and Offending

bullets.text: West: 20% of those with IQ<90 become delinquent vs 9% (IQ 91–98) vs 2% (IQ>110). Lyall: only 2% of 358 adults with LD in residential/day services had police contact in a year, with marked underreporting. Harris: aggressive behaviour prevalence 17.6% overall (9.7% day hospital, 38.2% inpatient). Prison LD prevalence varies 2–40% across studies; LD offenders in high-secure care have the longest stays and are hardest to discharge.

People with LD are more likely to commit sexual or fire-raising offences, though property offences remain the most common overall (Hodgins); offending is more likely in mild/moderate than severe LD. Sex offenders with ID more often target younger male children; Hawk found sex-offence charge rates nearly twice as high in intellectually disabled vs non-disabled defendants.

Reoffending rates are 40–70% untreated, falling to 20–55% after treatment (comparable to non-LD offenders); recidivism risk is highest in the year immediately post-discharge. Management uses group Sex Offender Treatment Programmes plus pharmacotherapy (SSRI/anti-libidinal agents).

condensedNotes.heading: Other Psychiatric Conditions & Offending

bullets.text: Mood disorders: bipolar disorder's link to violence is unclear, and if present is much lower magnitude (~1/10th) than schizophrenia's. Depression is a risk factor for violence mainly alongside other risk factors (psychosis, substance use) and is a clear risk factor for domestic killings; psychotic depression can produce nihilism leading to 'mercy killings' within a domestic/family setting.

Anxiety disorders occur in 10–25% of prisoners with little direct evidence of an offending link, though severe anxiety can cause dissociation/disinhibition. Dissociative/conversion disorders can occur under stress in non-disordered individuals (e.g. soldiers); dissociative/psychogenic amnesia is associated with violence to a known victim where the perpetrator is often aroused or intoxicated — such amnesia is difficult to give clear legal evidence about.

Epilepsy: ~1% general population prevalence, 1–2% in prison, with no general increase in violent acts; ictal violence is rare and more likely in partial than tonic-clonic seizures. Related concepts referenced in the literature: episodic dyscontrol syndrome (amnesia for explosive violence) and intermittent explosive disorder (DSM).

Asperger's syndrome frequently overlaps with schizoid PD; some studies show more violent offences/criminal damage than the general population, attributed to theory-of-mind deficits, egocentricity and social-reciprocity deficits — especially relevant to sexual offending, though there is no particular increase in violent sexual offences.

Sleep disorders/parasomnias are commoner in children; when violence occurs in this context it is commoner in males, usually with a prior parasomnia history (including nocturnal enuresis), with sleep deprivation/cannabis/alcohol/caffeine as precursors. The sleepwalking offender usually knows the victim, and appears not to hear cries or recognise the victim during the episode.

condensedNotes.heading: Special Forensic Syndromes

bullets.text: Malingering is intentional feigning of symptoms for a specific gain; assessment tools include SIRS, SIMS (structured inventories of reported/malingered symptoms) and the TOMM (test of malingered memory); polygraphs are used in the US but rarely the UK.

Munchausen syndrome is a factitious illness with intentionally created symptoms to assume the sick role without external incentive (specified as psychological or physical); Munchausen-by-proxy is factitious illness induced in a child/dependent. Associated with personality disorder, attention-seeking, masochistic and medication-seeking behaviours; management involves safeguarding, treating any depression, and limiting behaviours (e.g. a hospital register).

Morbid jealousy (Othello syndrome) has a core belief of the partner's infidelity, commonest with paranoid PD or an underlying psychotic condition, often with confirmatory behaviours (stalking, repeated calls); significant risks include partner/child harm, self-harm, substance misuse, domestic violence and homicide.

Erotomania (De Clerambault's syndrome) is commoner in females — the belief that someone (often more successful) is in love with them, associated with psychotic disorders; Mullen (2008) links it to stalking or evolving pathological jealousy, with violence occurring on rejection of the perpetrator.

Ganser syndrome is a hysterical dissociative disorder featuring approximate answers, clouding of consciousness with disorientation, psychogenic physical symptoms (analgesia/hyperaesthesia) and pseudohallucinations (not all features always present); patients are amnesic for the abnormal behaviour. It is often seen in prisoners, especially military prisoners and those absenting themselves from the army/navy.

condensedNotes.heading: Special Offender Groups — Women, Young Offenders, Ethnic Minorities & Deaf Offenders

bullets.text: Only 1 in 5 offenders is a woman (male:female conviction ratio ~5:1); women's peak offending age is 2–3 years earlier than men's (14 vs 17–18). Women's index offence is more often 'romantic'/domestic; 68% of imprisoned women are there for non-violent offences (vs 47% of men); women steal fewer/lower-value items and receive more psychiatric pleas and disposals than men.

Women in custody are 5x more likely to have mental health problems than women in the general population; up to 80% have diagnosable mental health problems, and 1 in 5 remand women (2003) had psychosis. HMIP (2006/07): 19% of women had attempted suicide in the year before custody (~3x the male rate); 33% had an accommodation need; 31% had an alcohol misuse problem (vs 42% of men); 60% had emotional wellbeing problems recorded (vs 36% of men).

Age of criminal responsibility: 10 (England & Wales), 8 (Scotland). Juvenile offenders are 10–17, young offenders 18–21, adult offenders ≥21, handled via the youth offending service. Placement options: Young Offender Institutes (18–21, and 15–17 for juveniles), secure training centres/detention schools (up to 17), secure children's homes (12–16), adolescent secure hospitals.

Ethnic minority groups make up 15% of the UK population but are overrepresented in prison and secure settings, with documented concerns about more schizophrenia diagnoses, more involuntary admission, more seclusion/restraint, and more custodial sentences among BME patients.

Deaf offenders have a higher prevalence of mental disorder and face communication-related barriers to services; the UK has three general psychiatric hospitals, one high-secure deaf service and several independent hospitals providing inpatient care. Deafness may affect an individual's fitness to plead.

condensedNotes.heading: Victims of Crime & Patients as Victims

bullets.text: Crime victimisation impairs occupational, parenting, relationship and general social functioning; non-violent crime has relatively little impact on life satisfaction, but the more violent the crime, the greater the social dysfunction. Sexual assault victims are particularly prone to social withdrawal (Golding et al. 2002); >50% report a continuously restricted social life even 15–30 months after the assault.

PTSD is more frequent in the forensic population; there is no definite causal link between offending and PTSD in perpetrators, but both perpetrators and victims carry high PTSD risk (higher in victims) — ~20% of prisoners have diagnosable PTSD. Complex PTSD is associated with prolonged childhood abuse with common comorbid substance misuse; psychosis combined with PTSD can increase positive symptoms and paranoid/violent thoughts. The index offence itself can be a significant traumatic trigger for forensic inpatients in up to 70% of cases, especially if unplanned, the offender was disinhibited, and there was no prior forensic history.

Khalifeh et al. (2015), National Crime Survey: 40% of patients with severe mental illness were victims of crime in the past year vs 14% of the general population (OR 2.8); for violent assault specifically, 19% of patients vs 3% of controls (OR 5.3). Women with severe mental illness were 4x more likely to be victims of domestic violence, 4x more likely victims of sexual violence, and 10x more likely to be victims of any community violence.

condensedNotes.heading: Mental Health Act & the Criminal Justice Pathway (England & Wales)

bullets.text: Under PACE guidelines, an 'appropriate adult' must be informed and attend if a suspect is thought to have a mental disorder/disability; the Crown Prosecution Service continues prosecution only if the public interest outweighs other concerns.

Courts can remand to hospital under Section 35 for assessment (up to 28 days initially, maximum 12 weeks) to produce a report on mental disorder, or under the rarely-used Section 36 for treatment (28 days, renewable to 12 weeks total — only 16 recorded uses in England & Wales to March 2007). If the Crown Court finds the accused unfit to plead, a 'trial of facts' follows.

Disposals after a full trial or trial of facts: absolute discharge (acquittal), probation/health supervision order (conditional discharge), prison, or hospital disposal (with restriction/supervision/guardianship orders available in some cases). Section 37 guardianship orders are little used (supervision orders being more available); they last 6 months initially, renewable by the Responsible Clinician (RC) at 6 months then yearly, and empower the guardian to require residence, attendance for treatment/education, and access.

Section 41 restriction orders can be added to a hospital order in serious cases and have no time limit; an unrestricted hospital order lasts 6 months initially, renewable by the RC at 6 months then yearly. With a restriction order, the RC needs Ministry of Justice permission for leave/discharge and hospital managers cannot discharge unilaterally.

Sentenced prisoners needing hospital transfer use Section 47, typically with a Section 49 restriction direction preventing hospital-led discharge; on expiry of a fixed-term sentence, the Section 49 restriction is removed and the section 'notionally' converts to a Section 37.

condensedNotes.heading: Secure Settings, Care Models & Multi-Agency Working

bullets.text: High secure units hold MDOs of grave/immediate risk; medium secure units serve high-risk MDOs; low secure units hold MDOs with limited violence/absconding risk. Young Offender Institutes, detention schools (higher relational security than YOIs), secure children's homes (lower security) and adolescent secure hospitals (medium secure) exist for younger offenders.

Community care models: Parallel Care (inpatient medium secure care and community care run in parallel with the same service), Integrated Care (general psychiatric services take over long-term rehabilitation and lower-security readmissions post-discharge), and Hybrid Care (integrated model plus a period of 'shared care' post-discharge, with forensic services retaining long-term care for a subset of high-risk offenders).

~70% of supervised offenders in England & Wales are on probation on discharge from secure institutions. Probation officer roles: pre-sentence assessment, monitoring sentenced offenders, advising the parole board, supervising licence/recall, supervising/reporting breach of community sentences, advising on local resources, and directly providing psychological-programme support.

Prison inreach teams (now in ~87% of UK prisons) link to primary care. NOMS joins up prison and probation services and advises government on policy. MAPPA (Multi-Agency Public Protection Arrangements) covers MDOs convicted of a specified sexual/violent offence sentenced >12 months, or hospital-detained/conditionally discharged, providing an interagency framework for managing violent and sexual offenders.

Three security domains: physical (fences/locks, soft cutlery, removal of sharps/hanging points), relational (training, communication, meaningful activities — its absence undermines physical security), procedural (searches, incident learning, staff vetting, governance). Observation levels: general (location known, not in eyesight), intermittent, within eyesight (high/imminent risk), and within arm's length (highest risk of rapid self-harm, e.g. swallowing an object).

Section 17 leave decisions weigh mental state stability, insight, staff rapport, treatment engagement, and past leave behaviour; leave forms specify purpose/conditions, destination, escort availability and transport — this is distinct from parole.

condensedNotes.heading: Prison Psychiatry — Morbidity, Suicide & Self-harm

bullets.text: Mental disorder (including substance misuse) is found in 37% of sentenced men, 63% of remand men, 57% of sentenced women and 76% of remand women (Gunn 1991; Maden 1995); ~1/4 of remand men and 1/3 of remand women have ≥2 diagnoses. The commonest PD diagnosis in all four subgroups is antisocial PD, then paranoid PD. (See table for full ICD-10 diagnosis breakdown.)

Brugha et al.: probable functional psychosis prevalence was 4.5/1000 (~0.4%) in the household survey vs 52/1000 (~5.2%) in the prison survey — over 10x higher; ~1/4 of prison psychoses are attributable to psychoactive substances. Fazel & Danesh (2002) internationally: men 3.7% psychotic/10% MDD/65% PD (47% ASPD); women 4.0% psychotic/12% MDD/42% PD (21% ASPD); prisoners are ~20x more likely to have psychosis/major depression and ~10x more likely to have ASPD than the general population.

Prison suicide rate more than doubled 1982–1998 (54→128/100,000); self-inflicted deaths represent about half of all prison deaths, with local prisons bearing the higher brunt. The most common method is hanging; suicide is ~8x higher in prison than the general population; the majority occur within 6 months of imprisonment, and life-sentence prisoners are overrepresented. Alcohol/substance misuse is the most likely associated psychiatric problem; remand prisoners, young offenders and those with substance-misuse/violent-offence histories carry particular risk.

condensedNotes.heading: Violence Risk Assessment — Concepts, Approaches & Stages

bullets.text: The Butler Committee defined dangerousness as 'a propensity to cause serious physical injury or lasting psychological harm' — a term now replaced by risk assessment/management. The Ritchie report (Christopher Clunis's killing of Jonathan Zito) identified failures of individual-practitioner risk assessment and management.

Prediction problems: low base rate (serious violence measured at <1% even in the severely mentally ill — Wallace 1998) severely limits predictive value and raises false positives; risk is multifactorial, changes over time, and factor interactions are often unknown. Risk factors are static (fixed/historical, e.g. family history of suicide), stable (enduring but somewhat modifiable, e.g. PD diagnosis) or dynamic (fluctuating, e.g. acute anxiety/akathisia) — dynamic factors can multiply the effect of underlying static/stable factors if unaddressed.

Homicide inquiries have identified recurring problems: failure to consider carers' views, undue emphasis on patients' civil liberties, failure to properly implement the MHA, taking a cross-sectional rather than longitudinal view of risk, and failure to share information.

Three approaches: clinical (subjective/intuitive, poor predictive value — only ~1/3 of pure clinical judgments estimated correct retrospectively), actuarial (algorithmic numerical probability, superior for predicting violence/sexual reoffending but insensitive to change, high false-positive rate, poor cross-setting generalisation, over-weights static/stable factors), and structured professional judgment (combines evidence-based risk factors with individual clinical assessment, e.g. HCR-20). Neither actuarial nor structured judgment should replace conventional clinical assessment.

Bouch & Marshall's risk-assessment stages: (A) identify need for a full structured assessment, (B) assess static/stable/dynamic/future factors and protective factors, (C) formulate risk in the current context, (D) consider interventions/support level, (E) anticipate intervention impact, (F) develop a management plan with short/long-term actions, (G) review and revise as risk factors change.

condensedNotes.heading: Structured & Actuarial Risk Assessment Tools

bullets.text: HCR-20 (Webster) shows good inter-rater reliability, with 10 historical items (e.g. previous violence, PCL-R score), 5 clinical items (e.g. lack of insight, PD diagnosis) and 5 risk-management items (e.g. plan feasibility, lack of support); it predicts both inpatient and post-discharge community violence. (Full item breakdown in table.)
SARA is a 20-item structured guide for spousal-assault risk in men arrested for spousal assault; SVR-20 is a 20-item structured guide for assessing violence risk in sex offenders.

VRAG (Quinsey 1995, validated in Canadian prisons) is a 12-item actuarial tool entirely reliant on historical factors and includes PCL-R as a subscale. PCL-R (Hare) scores 0–40 (0–2 per item, 20 items); cutoff ≥25 diagnoses psychopathy, but PCL-R was not itself designed as a standalone actuarial risk tool. Static-99 (Hanson & Thornton) is a 10-item actuarial tool for adult male sexual offenders ≥18 at release. SORAG is a 14-item actuarial tool incorporating PCL-R. The Violence Risk Scale has 23 dynamic and 6 static variables.

condensedNotes.heading: Fitness to Plead & the R v Pritchard Criteria

bullets.text: Fitness to plead concerns mental ability to comply with trial proceedings; physical conditions (deafness/muteness) are also relevant. There is a presumption of fitness; the factors are relevant only at time of trial (not arrest/charging), and amnesia for the offence does not itself interfere with fitness to plead.

R v Pritchard criteria — a defendant is unfit to plead if incapable of: understanding the charge(s); deciding whether to plead guilty; exercising the right to challenge jurors; instructing solicitors/counsel; following the course of proceedings; giving evidence in their own defence.

Under the Criminal Procedures Act 1964, two medical practitioners must give evidence on fitness. If fitness is raised by the prosecution it must be proven 'beyond reasonable doubt'; if raised by the defence, on the 'balance of probabilities'. Trial can be delayed to allow treatment aimed at improving fitness. If found unfit, a 'trial of facts' proceeds and all disposals remain available.

condensedNotes.heading: McNaughten Rules, Diminished Responsibility & Capacity to Form Intent

bullets.text: McNaughten Rules (1843), 4 components: a defect of reason (impaired, not mere failure to exercise it); due to a disease of the mind (not externally caused); leading to loss of appreciation of the nature/quality of the act; such that the accused did not realise the act was wrong (legally or morally). Burden of proof lies with the defence; the jury decides; disposals remain flexible (not automatically hospital confinement).

Diminished responsibility reduces a murder charge to manslaughter; the defence must show absence of mens rea (act remains unlawful, but no malice aforethought). Disposal for murder is restricted, but flexible for manslaughter; females and those with no criminal record are more likely to have this defence granted.

Capacity to form intent: symptoms that can prevent formation of the relevant mental processes include specific relevant delusions, an abnormal mood state (severe depression/mania) with psychomotor change or impaired concentration, and severe cognitive impairment (dementia/chronic schizophrenia) — this excludes voluntary intoxication (doctrine of prior fault, as a person is expected to foresee this). If diminished capacity is upheld, acquittal or conviction for a lesser offence may follow.

condensedNotes.heading: Automatism, Culpable Homicide & Intoxication Defences

bullets.text: Automatism is a plea that the defendant's actions were not under conscious control (unwilled, involuntary bodily movements), negating the actus reus. It is a rare plea. Sane automatism (automatism simpliciter, extrinsic/one-off cause) leads to complete acquittal; insane automatism (intrinsic cause, likely to recur) leads to a not-guilty-by-reason-of-insanity type disposal. Courts limit the defence where the defendant exercised some control, the condition falls under insanity rules, or there was prior fault.

Hypoglycaemia (isolated), night terrors and dissociative states are classed as sane/'external' automatisms; sleepwalking, epilepsy and recurring hypoglycaemia as insane/'internal' automatisms. R v Burgess (1991) held somnambulism could be genetic/internal and thus classified as sane or insane at the judge's discretion.

Fenwick (1990) features supporting a sleepwalking-automatism defence: family/childhood history of sleepwalking; occurring within 2 hours of sleep onset (a non-REM phenomenon); witnessed inappropriate/confused behaviour; presence of triggers (alcohol, fatigue, sleep deprivation); substantial amnesia; no attempt to conceal the crime; lack of sexual arousal (e.g. penile erection) if the alleged offence is sexual.

Culpable homicide lies between manslaughter and murder: involuntary (unintended death from assault or negligence) or voluntary (intentional/reckless act mitigated by provocation or diminished responsibility).

Intoxication is rarely used as a defence. Involuntary intoxication (a spiked drink, a prescribed medication's effect, reckless use of a non-dangerous substance, or an irresistible dependence-driven impulse) is a valid defence/mitigating factor; voluntary self-induced intoxication is not a defence.

condensedNotes.heading: Mitigating Factors & Amnesia for the Offence

bullets.text: Mitigating factors reducing culpability: provocation, age/vulnerability, mental disorder or LD, involuntary intoxication, remorse, and a limited role in the offence.

Kopelman (2002): amnesia is commonly claimed in violent offences, especially homicide (25–45% of occasions); other associated conditions include psychosis, epilepsy, hysterical personality traits, parasomnias, organic brain disorder, hypoglycaemia and head injury. Amnesia itself has no legal implication in England & Wales absent automatism, and does not render someone unfit to plead — though credibility issues can arise without expert-witness support, particularly for fitness to plead/to be interviewed and reliability of an amnesic syndrome.

condensedNotes.heading: The Psychiatrist's Role — Evidence, Reports, Expert Witnesses & Human Rights

bullets.text: The case-law test for fitness to give evidence: understanding the question, applying one's mind to answering it, and conveying answers intelligibly to the jury. Three types of false confession are recognised: voluntary, coerced-compliant, coerced-internalised — influenced by situational factors (custody/isolation/interrogation) and individual factors (mental disorder, incapacity); assessment involves reviewing transcripts and vulnerability/cognitive/intelligence/disorder factors.

Key psychiatric roles in the criminal justice pathway: assessing suspects in custody, advising on mental-health diversion and medical needs, advising on fitness to be interviewed and need for an appropriate adult, advising on fitness to plead/stand trial, arranging remand-to-hospital transfer, and advising on sentencing options.

GMC good-practice principles for reports (2006, paras 63, 65–67): be honest and trustworthy; ensure documents are not false or misleading, taking reasonable steps to verify information and not deliberately omitting relevant information; act without unreasonable delay; be honest in all spoken/written evidence and make clear the limits of one's knowledge/competence.

Three witness types: ordinary (witness to fact, not opinion), professional (comments on clinical state with some prior involvement), expert (writes reports/statements on mental disorder or a specific issue) — expert witnesses provide advisory, actuarial, clinical or experimental expertise.

ECHR articles most relevant to forensic practice: Article 2 (right to life — the state has a positive duty to safeguard prisoners/those in custody), Article 3 (prohibition of torture/degrading treatment), Article 5 (right to personal liberty — authorises detention of persons of 'unsound mind'; underpins the deprivation of liberty safeguards), Article 8 (right to private and family life, widely interpreted).

examinerTraps.text: Pritchard criteria are about capacity to engage with the trial process (understanding the charge, deciding plea, challenging jurors, instructing counsel, following proceedings, giving evidence) — they do NOT include an ability to distinguish diminished responsibility from automatism, a plausible-sounding but wrong distractor.

examinerTraps.text: Amnesia for the offence does NOT itself render a defendant unfit to plead — the exam favours a defendant with amnesia as 'most likely to be fit to plead' over one who is catatonic/mute or cannot understand charges/procedure.

Alcohol/drug problems are more strongly linked to violence than any single mental illness category.

examinerTraps.text: Two near-identically worded SBAs on 'the greatest risk factor for suicide in prison' give different single-best-answers depending on the option set offered — 'occupying a single cell' in one, 'history of substance misuse' in another. Both are genuine risk factors in the source material; the lesson is that the 'correct' answer is contingent on which distractors accompany it, not an absolute ranking — read the full option list before answering.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Forensics Part 1_ Attempt review.pdf

examinerTraps.text: Voluntary intoxication can NEVER found an insanity plea or defence to a basic-intent crime (e.g. sexual assault) — even when it directly precipitated the offence. Contrast with involuntary intoxication (spiked drink, prescribed medication, reckless use of a non-dangerous substance, dependence-driven irresistible impulse), which IS a valid defence/mitigating factor.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Forensics Part 1_ Attempt review.pdf

examinerTraps.text: Supporting sleepwalking-as-automatism is a specific feature list — offence within 2 hours of sleep onset (a non-REM phenomenon), family history, witnessed confusion, presence of triggers (alcohol/fatigue), substantial amnesia, no concealment, and no sexual arousal if the offence is sexual. The exam tests the exact detail ('within 2 hours') rather than a vague 'recent sleep' distractor.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Forensics Part 1_ Attempt review.pdf

examinerTraps.text: Sane vs insane automatism is classified by INTRINSIC vs EXTRINSIC cause, not by severity or degree of consciousness impairment — sleep terrors are 'sane' (extrinsic), while sleepwalking (R v Burgess) was held capable of being 'insane'/internal (genetic) despite superficially resembling other parasomnias.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Forensics Part 1_ Attempt review.pdf

examinerTraps.text: The single best predictor of a FUTURE sexual offence is a history of PREVIOUS sexual offences — not the severity of the current offence or a specific diagnosis.

This nuance — structured (HCR-20/SARA/SVR-20) vs actuarial (VRAG/PCL-R-as-subscale/Static-99/SORAG) vs 'diagnostic-not-actuarial' PCL-R — is tested across both SBA and EMI formats.

examinerTraps.text: Penrose's Law/hypothesis specifically describes the INVERSE relationship between the number of psychiatric beds and the prison population — it is not a direct claim that mental illness causes crime, a subtly different (and wrong) paraphrase often offered as a distractor.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Forensics Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

examinerTraps.text: Legal-terminology precision is heavily tested: actus reus = the (voluntary) physical act; mens rea = intent; doli incapax = incapable of crime (below age of criminal responsibility); habeas corpus = right to a hearing on the legality of detention; corpus delicti = the factual evidence/body of the offence. These near-synonymous Latin terms are deliberately confused as both single-best-answer and EMI matching items.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Forensics Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

examinerTraps.text: Stalking typology hinges on a subtle distinction: 'rejected' stalkers HAD a prior relationship and pursue reconciliation/vengeance, whereas 'intimacy seekers' had NO prior relationship but believe an imagined love will be reciprocated — both involve a hoped-for relationship, making them easy to conflate. Tested in both SBA and EMI formats.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Forensics Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

examinerTraps.text: Impulse control disorders are distinguished by demographic stereotype as much as by symptom: kleptomania (typically women in their 30s), pyromania (more often male adolescents with poor social skills/learning difficulties), trichotillomania and pathological gambling each carry a distinct typical profile — the exam expects you to match the vignette demographic, not just the behaviour.

examinerTraps.text: Disposal outcome tracks diagnosis, not just offence severity: among homicide perpetrators with a personality disorder as the primary diagnosis, 92% are imprisoned and only ~4% receive a hospital disposal — almost the mirror image of schizophrenia-primary perpetrators (29% imprisoned, 71% hospital order). A classic cross-cutting legal/clinical trap.

gaps.subtopic: Mental Health Act 1983 (as amended) — exact current section numbers and safeguards
gaps.note: The source notes explicitly state that detailed knowledge of exact MHA sections/articles is NOT required for the MRCPsych exam and present only a reference flowchart; subsequent reforms to the 1983 Act are not covered here. Verify any exact section number, time limit, or safeguard you plan to rely on against the current Mental Health Act and its Code of Practice.

gaps.subtopic: Mental Capacity Act / Court of Protection mechanics
gaps.note: Only a single EMI item mentions a Court of Protection order; no Mental Capacity Act framework (best-interests test, Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards/Liberty Protection Safeguards process, capacity assessment steps) is covered in these source notes — verify against the MCA 2005 and its Code of Practice.

gaps.subtopic: Dosing and monitoring of anti-libidinal/testosterone-lowering agents
gaps.note: The source describes the mechanisms and headline side effects of cyproterone acetate, medroxyprogesterone acetate and GnRH agonists, but gives no dosing, monitoring schedule, or current UK licensing status. Verify against the Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines (15th ed.) before applying this to any prescribing-style question.

gaps.subtopic: Current full ICD-11/DSM-5 diagnostic criteria text
gaps.note: The notes and questions reference ICD-10/ICD-11/DSM-IV/DSM-5 category names (kleptomania, pyromania, conduct-dissocial disorder, paraphilic disorder) but do not reproduce complete current criteria sets. Verify exact current diagnostic criteria against ICD-11/DSM-5 directly rather than relying on this summary.

gaps.subtopic: Current NICE guidance on violence/aggression management and personality disorder treatment
gaps.note: These notes do not cite current NICE guidance (e.g. on violence and aggression management, or on borderline/antisocial personality disorder treatment) for risk-management or PD-treatment recommendations. Verify current NICE guidance directly before relying on this guide for management-of-violence questions.

Several figures (domestic violence reporting rates, homicide-by-MDO trend data, prison suicide rates) derive from British Crime Survey/Home Office data and SPMM course text dated up to roughly the early-2010s. Treat these as the figures the exam bank tests rather than as current statistics, and cross-check against current ONS/Ministry of Justice data before using them clinically.
